concept.name: Commodity
concept.definition: As defined in the Commodity Exchange Act, the agricultural commodities enumerated in Section 1a(9) plus all other goods and articles (onions excepted) and all services, rights, and interests in which contracts for future delivery are presently or in the future dealt in. In everyday market usage, a physical commodity is a fungible raw good — an agricultural product, metal, or energy product — traded in standardized grades, as opposed to a financial instrument.
concept.intuition: A commodity is a standardized raw input: one bushel of No. 2 yellow corn or one troy ounce of gold is interchangeable with another, which is what makes them tradeable in bulk.
concept.mechanics: Commodities trade in cash (spot) markets and through futures, forwards, options, and swaps on designated contract markets and OTC. Prices are driven by production, inventories, weather, geopolitics, and the costs of storage, insurance, and financing (the cost of carry), which shape the futures curve into contango or backwardation.
concept.failure_modes: Physical supply shocks, storage and transport constraints, and delivery bottlenecks can produce extreme price moves, squeezes, or even negative prices. For hedgers, the legal definition is broader than the everyday one — interest rates and stock indexes are also 'commodities' under the CEA — which catches the unwary in regulatory scope questions.
concept.misconceptions: That 'commodity' means only physical raw materials; under the Commodity Exchange Act it includes virtually anything on which futures trade, including financial benchmarks. Also, commodity prices are not determined by futures markets alone — cash supply and demand anchor them.
concept.example: No. 2 yellow corn is a fungible commodity: a farmer sells 5,000 bushels at the local elevator's cash price, while a processor hedges future purchases with corn futures.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
